newsitem.title: USA: Fed likely to raise rates before yearend -- Analysts.
newsitem.headline: Fed likely to raise rates before yearend -- Analysts.

text.p: The Federal Reserve, after giving U.S. growth and job markets another chance, is now expected to raise short-term interest rates before the end of the year, U.S. analysts said on Tuesday.

"The Fed continues to focus on good inflation numbers rather than on the (future) inflation scenario," said chief economist Steve Ricchiuto at Barclays Wedd de Zoete Government Securities. "Clearly, the Fed feels confident the upticks in wages reflect higher productivity. That's good news for the economy and good news for the market as well."
The Federal Open Market Committee met on Tuesday and decided to leave the 5.25-percent federal funds rate and the 5.0-percent discount rate unchanged. Both rates have held since January 31.
Ricchiuto, whose firm had anticipated an aggressive 50-point move on both federal funds and discount rates, said the Fed is likely to raise rates later this year "if these growth numbers continue."
The U.S. Gross Domestic Product grew at a 4.8-percent pace in the second quarter and the unemployment rate fell to a seven-year low of 5.1 percent.
"They (Fed officials) are not moving as quickly as they should," contended Ricchiuto, who forecast a rate hike later this year due to inflationary risks of a full-employment environment.

Suzanne Rizzo, U.S. economist at the advisory firm MFR Inc., agreed "there is a very high probability they will do it (tighten credit) after the (presidential) elections, barring a major change in the trend of the economic indicators."
Rizzo said the Fed will need to tighten credit in the near term out of concern for the possibility of wage pressures feeding into overall inflation.
Analysts estimate that labor costs account for roughly two-thirds of consumer inflation.
Rizzo said the Fed is bound to raise rates before the end of the year unless a second-half slowdown materializes as forecast by the Fed Board staff.
"We would have to see a far more pronounced weakening in the employment data, wage pressures, or final demand data than what we have seen so far," Rizzo added.
Wrightson and Associates chief economist Lou Crandall said the absence of a move now raises the odds for an aggressive hike in November -- or even for an inter-meeting move.

"The absence of a move today raises the odds of a half-point move in November. An inter-meeting move is unlikely but not unconceivable if the economic data prove problematic," said Crandall who saw an outside chance of a move before the next November 13 FOMC meeting.

"But it would take a surprise on a number of indicators (for an inter-meeting move)," added Crandall who forecast that special factors may skew the next CPI upward. "The CPI itself won't do it. You also would have to get much stronger employment and retail numbers for the Fed to move inter-meeting."
